title: Sri Lanka Deploys Air Force Drones as Worst Dengue Outbreak in a Decade Kills 53
excerpt: With more than 76,000 infections and hospitals comparing the surge to COVID-era peaks, the island nation has mobilised its military to hunt mosquito-breeding sites using drone surveillance.
body:
• Sri Lanka is battling its worst dengue outbreak in nearly a decade, with 76,044 infections and 53 deaths since January, driven by the more virulent DENV-2 strain
  • The air force has deployed drones to identify mosquito-breeding rooftop water pools, while military and police teams inspect homes and clear breeding sites
  • Hospitals are overwhelmed — doctors in Colombo compare the surge to COVID-19 peaks, with patients sharing beds and some treated on floors
  • The crisis comes months after Cyclone Ditwah devastated infrastructure, and authorities are weighing a dengue vaccine though efficacy concerns remain

Sri Lanka has mobilised its armed forces, including air force drones, to fight a spiralling dengue outbreak that has overwhelmed hospitals and infected more than 76,000 people since January — the worst the island nation has seen in nearly a decade.

Scale of the Crisis

With 53 deaths and 76,044 infections as of mid-July, the outbreak is approaching the tally of more than 100,000 cases recorded during Sri Lanka's catastrophic 2017 dengue season, which killed 440 people, according to Reuters. About 75 percent of current cases are linked to the more virulent DENV-2 strain, which produces more severe symptoms and spreads more rapidly.

https://x.com/WIONews/status/2079785888473833959

The surge accelerated sharply in June, when 21,537 cases were recorded — more than double the May figure. The first two weeks of July brought an additional 18,000 cases, with more than 1,000 patients admitted to hospitals daily, according to health authorities.

"It's challenging for the doctors because it's a rapid increase in patients. All of a sudden, you get a large influx coming into the hospital."

— Dr. Lalindra Dias, consultant at Negombo District General Hospital

Military Intervention

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake ordered the deployment of army, navy, and air force personnel to join a special unit focused on identifying and destroying mosquito-breeding sites. Air force drones are being used to survey rooftops where monsoon rainwater has pooled, creating ideal conditions for Aedes mosquitoes to breed.

Nearly 11,000 mosquito-breeding sites have been cleared this month, with fines levied at more than 4,000 premises found to harbour them, according to the health ministry. Laws are being strictly enforced against property owners who allow breeding conditions to persist.

The air force is also helping overstretched staff at some public hospitals to manage patient tracking systems, as medical facilities buckle under the case load.

Hospitals Under Strain

The healthcare system is under extraordinary pressure. Dengue specialist Professor Neelika Malavige of the University of Sri Jayewardenepura compared the situation to COVID-19 surges, telling media that "hospitals are absolutely full, in public hospitals you have two patients per bed and in some hospitals there are even patients on the floor."

The Negombo District General Hospital treated nearly 1,800 patients in less than two months since June, up from about 1,050 in all of 2022, according to Reuters. Public health workers are "stretched to their limit," said Kapila Kannangara, acting director general of the National Dengue Control Unit.

To reduce hospital burden, doctors are advising patients with mild symptoms to recover at home. "The doctor asked me to stay at home because my platelet count had not fallen too much," 23-year-old Shalini Aloka Perera told Reuters.

Compounding Factors

The dengue crisis arrives on the heels of Cyclone Ditwah, which struck in late November and caused an estimated $1.4 billion in damage, according to World Bank estimates. The cyclone destroyed critical health infrastructure and created debris and standing water that accelerated mosquito breeding.

Sri Lanka's advantage of four hospital beds per 1,000 people — above the global average of fewer than three — is being tested by the dual pressures of cyclone recovery and the dengue surge. Monsoon rains, flooding, and haphazardly dumped waste have created ideal conditions for Aedes mosquito proliferation across the island's western and southern regions.

Vaccine Debate and Outlook

Authorities are considering introducing a dengue vaccine, though experts have warned it may offer limited benefits given the complexity of the virus and the multiple strains currently circulating. The debate mirrors similar deliberations in other South Asian nations grappling with dengue's expanding geographic range due to climate change.

Health officials expect infections to ease as monsoon rains weaken in August, but warn that cases could climb again from November when the island's second annual monsoon season begins. Dr. Dias cautioned that the virulence of DENV-2 makes predictions difficult: "We cannot exactly say when it will stop."

The World Health Organization has warned that dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases are spreading faster and farther globally due to climate change — a pattern with direct relevance to South Asia's densely populated coastal regions, where many members of the Indian and Sri Lankan diasporas have family ties.
